The comparison with 50 shots shows where the choice of interval matters (§15):

Near the pole the delta method covers the true value in fewer than one experiment in ten; Wilson and the Haar posterior recover the nominal coverage. On Haar states the posterior mean has a 4% lower mean squared error than the raw frequency.
Figure 4.2 shows the cause in milli-qang. With 50 shots, the width of the delta-method interval drops to zero at the ends of the scale: with 50 zeros in 50 shots it gives \([+1000,+1000]\) m-qg, an interval with no width. With 48 zeros it gives \([+811,+1029]\) m-qg, which runs off the top of the scale. Wilson gives \([+731,+978]\) and Bayes–Haar \(+885\) \([+731,+975]\) m-qg: widths that do not collapse and stay inside \([-1000,+1000]\).






Figure 4.2: Width of the 95 % interval with 50 shots, in milli-qang, against the estimate. The delta method collapses at the poles; Wilson and Bayes–Haar do not.



The honest reading of the table has two parts. The Haar prior repairs the collapse of the delta method and has a clean geometric justification; but the Wilson interval, standard in statistics, achieves the same coverage, and the gain over good frequentist practice is in the point estimate and is modest. The qg unit does not reduce the number of shots a given precision requires; what it brings is making the cost explicit and choosing the interval well.

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.4 Second-order unbiased estimators
Quadratic quantities have a systematic bias. The plug-in estimator \(\widehat{qg}^{\,2}\) overestimates \(qg^2\) by \((1-qg^2)/N\), because shot noise always adds variance. The correction is exact:
\[
\widehat{qg^2}=\frac{N\,\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1}{N-1},\qquad \mathbb E\big[\widehat{qg^2}\big]=qg^2 ,
\]
valid for \(N\ge2\) (qg2_unbiased). It can go negative when \(qg\approx0\), the price of being unbiased. With \(N=20\) and \(qg=0.6\), the plug-in estimator averages 0.390 and the corrected one 0.358, against the true value 0.36.
It matters because the Bloch radius of Chapter 5, \(r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2\), is a sum of squares: without the correction each axis adds its bias, and an entangled state looks purer than it is (§97). The same correction enters the reading of the gravitational redshift with two clocks (§126, Chapter 8).

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.5 Planning the shots
The inverse relation, how many shots a given error needs, is the one used when preparing an experiment. plan_shots turns a target standard error of the filtered \(qg_Z\) into shots and estimated processor seconds, taking into account the fraction of shots the filter will keep (§143). For a target of 0.02 (20 m-qg) on two circuits per device it planned 3000–3400 shots, and over 30 repetitions the error of the worst qubit was 0.021–0.023 (21–23 m-qg): the plan held. For reference, Chapter 1’s formula without the filter gives \(N=(1000\sin\theta/\delta)^2=2500\) shots for 20 m-qg on the equator; the plan asks for more because it discounts the shots the filter will discard. The simple rule is \(N_\text{run}=N/(1-P_\text{discard})\): with a 20 % discard, the 2500 useful shots ask for 3125.
The per-qubit prediction, however, was 1.4–1.6 times optimistic on average, and its analysis is instructive: the qubits that missed were those near a pole (\(|qg|>0.8\), with ratios of 2.4–3.1), whose \(qg_Z\) the noise pulls away from \(\pm1\) and whose real variance is larger than the ideal one. The plan uses the worst qubit and therefore holds; the safe option, assuming no value of qg, is to plan for the worst case, \(qg=0\). The author’s working version attributes that excess to the curvature \(\kappa_{qg}=1000\,\lvert qg_Z\rvert\) of Chapter 1, largest at the poles: a random pulse error shifts the reading towards the equator in proportion to \(\kappa_{qg}\), and there the binomial variance is larger. It is an interpretation consistent with Chapter 1, but it was not tested on the data of §143.

The full Bloch vector is \((qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\), one per measurement axis. With 10 shots per axis, six estimators were compared on 2000 states (§35). The qg version applies the Haar prior axis by axis, \(\hat r_a=(2k_a-N)/(N+2)\), and projects onto the ball:

Linear inversion gives unphysical states in 52–88% of the runs on pure states. On mixed states the qg-Haar estimator is the best closed form (12–29% below maximum likelihood); on pure states its shrinkage towards the centre is a mistake, and it loses to maximum likelihood, by up to 50% near a pole. The right prior depends on which states are expected.
Would classical shadows (random Pauli measurements) do better than measuring the bases directly? For the quantities qang uses, no (§62). With exact per-shot variances on 6-qubit states, shadows need 3–41 times more shots for the same error: 3.0–4.3× for all the \(qg_Z\), 5.8–8.1× for the register-mean weight witness, 9–12.6× for all the \(ZZ\) correlators and 41× for the filtered imbalance. They only match direct measurement when the target is all one- and two-qubit quantities at once. And the shot-level filter does not exist with shadows: only \(3^{-6}=0.14\%\) of the random shots have every qubit measured in \(Z\).

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.7 The foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
A conceptual question remains: why \(qg_Z\) and not some other function of the populations? The operators of an \(n\)-qubit register form a finite-dimensional Hilbert space under the Hilbert–Schmidt product \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger B)\), and density matrices live in it. The Riesz–Fréchet representation theorem says that every continuous linear functional \(f\) on a Hilbert space has the form \(f(x)=\langle y_f,x\rangle\) for a unique \(y_f\); in finite dimension continuity is automatic and the theorem reduces to linear algebra (Appendix F).
The application is immediate. \(\rho\mapsto qg_Z(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\) is linear in \(\rho\), so it has a unique representative, \(\sigma_z\). Every linear read-out of a state (an expectation value, a population, a per-shot average) has that form, and \(qg_Z\) is the one whose representative is the \(Z\) observable. By contrast, \(qg_S(\rho)=H(\langle0|\rho|0\rangle)\) is strictly concave in \(\rho\): no operator represents it. Two properties already seen follow from this structural fact: linear functionals have unbiased sample-mean estimators and the entropy does not (Jensen’s inequality), and the identity \(qg_S=H((1+qg_Z)/2)\) shows that \(qg_S\) carries no information about the state beyond what the representative of \(qg_Z\) already extracts.
The milli-qang inherits this property: \(m(\rho)=1000\,\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\) is linear too, with representative \(1000\,\sigma_z\), which is why its estimator is the shot average, without bias. It is the underlying reason Chapter 1 defined the unit on probability and not on angle: \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\) is not linear in \(\rho\), has no representative and its direct estimator is biased. The same holds for the angle on the qga scale of Chapter 1: it is the same \(\theta\) multiplied by \(1000/2\pi\), so the angular scale changes the unit of the angle but does not make it linear in \(\rho\).
Open proposals. The author’s working version adds three proposals to this chapter, which the book records as unverified: watching the Fisher information \(qg_F=4000\,\operatorname{Var}(\sigma_z)\) so that an ansatz does not approach a global Haar 2-design (that the Haar measure over all of \(SU(2^n)\) produces barren plateaus is a known result (McClean et al. 2018); that \(qg_F\) serves to watch it is not); shot-noise propagation formulas for the regularized energy and the radiation function of Chapter 1, which depend on penalties not yet defined; and that the natural gradient in qg canonically diagonalizes the Fubini–Study tensor, which is true only for the coordinates \((\theta,\varphi)\) of one qubit (Section 1.4).

text:
4.8 The derived quantities in sampling
The treatise’s formulation brings the derived quantities of Chapter 1 (Section 1.11) to sampling. All of them are estimated from the same counts, and each one inherits a statistical property of this chapter.
Two Fisher informations. A shot carries about the polar bias the information \(F_{qg}=1/(1-qg_Z^2)\), which diverges at the poles, and about the qang angle \(F_\theta=1\), constant. They are the same information in two coordinates, and the information curvature is the first one in bits: \(qg_\kappa=F_{qg}/\ln2\).
Signal-to-noise and curvature when all shots agree. The plug-in estimators of \(qg_{SNR}\) and \(qg_\kappa\) divide by \(1-\widehat{qg}_Z^{\,2}\) and become infinite when the \(N\) shots coincide, which is exactly the case of Section 4.3. The Bayes–Haar posterior mean keeps them finite: with 50 out of 50, \(qg_Z=50/52=0.962\), \(qg_{SNR}=3.50\) and \(qg_\kappa=19.1\).
The geodesic distance between two samples. With \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) shots, each qang angle has variance \(1/N\), so
\[
\widehat{qg}_L=\frac{\lvert\hat\theta_1-\hat\theta_2\rvert}{2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\big(\widehat{qg}_L\big)\approx\frac14\left(\frac1{N_1}+\frac1{N_2}\right),
\]
wherever the two states are. It is half of Cohen’s \(h\), the classical effect size for comparing two proportions, so the test is not qang’s: qang gives it the name of a distance. With 750 and 700 zeros in 1000 shots each, \(\widehat{qg}_L=0.056\) rad (8.9 qga) with standard error \(0.0224\): a difference of 2.5σ. What Chapter 1 said holds: on a common meridian it is the Fubini–Study distance; with different azimuths, a lower bound.
The dissipative deficit from counts. \(qg_\tau=\sqrt{1-r^2}\) is a quadratic quantity, and it inherits the bias of Section 4.4 with the opposite sign. With \(N\) shots per axis, the plug-in radius satisfies
\[
\mathbb E\big[\hat r^{\,2}\big]=r^2+\frac{3-r^2}{N},
\]
so shot noise makes the state look purer than it is. A pure state measured with 100 shots per axis averages \(\hat r^{\,2}=1.02\), outside the sphere. A state with \(r=0.9\) (\(qg_\tau=0.436\)) averages \(\hat r^{\,2}=0.832\) with the plug-in estimator and \(0.810\) with the corrected one, which is the true value. The square root, however, is not unbiased even with the correction: \(\widehat{qg}_\tau\) averages \(0.376\) with the plug-in radius and \(0.404\) with the corrected one, both below \(0.436\), because the root is concave and is clipped at zero. The formulation proposes \(\sqrt{\max(0,1-\hat r^{\,2})}\) as an unbiased estimator; the corrected one halves the bias, it does not remove it.

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.11 Summary

\(\widehat{qg}_Z\) is unbiased and attains the Cramér–Rao bound; the delta method collapses near the poles, where its m-qg interval loses its width or runs off the scale.
Under the Haar measure \(qg_Z\) is uniform on \([-1,1]\), that is, uniform in milli-qang and in \(p_0\); the matching prior is \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) and gives exact intervals with a beta function.
Wilson and Bayes–Haar recover the nominal coverage where the delta method covers less than 10%; neither reduces the shots required.
Quadratic quantities need the correction \((N\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1)/(N-1)\); without it, Bloch radii are overestimated.
Of the derived quantities, \(qg_L\) between two samples is half of Cohen’s \(h\), with variance \(\tfrac14(1/N_1+1/N_2)\); \(qg_\tau\) estimated from counts stays biased low even with the quadratic correction.
Planning on the worst qubit meets the target; the qubits near a pole are the ones the noise pulls away most.
For qang’s quantities, measuring directly in \(Z\) costs 3–41 times fewer shots than classical shadows.
\(qg_Z\), and with it the milli-qang, is the canonical linear read-out by the Riesz–Fréchet theorem; \(qg_S\) and the angle are not linear and have no representative.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.1 The probability equation with a radius
Actualizado: 13 de noviembre de 2026 · Updated: November 13, 2026
Part I treated the qubit as a point on the surface of the sphere: a pure state, a probability \(p_0\) and its four readings. A qubit that belongs to a register is almost never pure: it is mixed by noise or by its entanglement with the others, and it sits inside the sphere. This chapter adds to the base of Chapter 1 the missing quantity, the local radius \(r\), and shows that the probability equation still holds with a single change: the polar bias is no longer \(\cos\theta\) but \(r\cos\theta\). From the radius come an entanglement measure, a way to separate the direction of the state from its purity, and wave–particle duality, all read in qg units.
For a qubit in a mixed state, its Bloch vector \((qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\) has length \(r\le1\), and Born’s rule in the \(Z\) basis reads
\[
p_0=\frac{1+qg_Z}{2}=\frac{1+r\cos\theta}{2}.
\]
It is the probability equation of Chapter 1 with the radius inside: the readings \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\) and \(m=2000\,p_0-1000\) m-qg do not change, but they no longer fix the angle, because the same \(p_0\) can come from a tilted pure state or from a mixed one closer to the pole. Each axis has its own probability, \(p_0^{(a)}\) in the basis \(a\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), and the squared radius is the sum of the three readings squared (§97):
\[
r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2=\frac{m_X^2+m_Y^2+m_Z^2}{10^6}=2\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2-1 .
\]
The radius is linear in the purity \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2\): it is 1 on the surface (pure state) and 0 at the centre (maximally mixed state). The sphere of radius \(r\) has area \(4\pi r^2\), and the surface deficit \(4\pi(1-r^2)\) is the area the qubit has lost; the library works with \(1-r^2\), which carries the same information.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
section: 5.2 The deficit as an entanglement measure
text:
5.2 The deficit as an entanglement measure
If the whole register is in a pure state, all the radius a qubit lacks is due to its entanglement with the rest. Then \(1-r_q^2=4\det\rho_q\) is the one-tangle of qubit \(q\), which for two qubits is the squared concurrence (Coffman et al. 2000), and its mean over the qubits is the global entanglement of Meyer and Wallach (2002):
\[
Q=\frac1n\sum_q\left(1-r_q^2\right).
\]
Two examples set the scale. In the Bell state each qubit sits at the centre of its sphere, \(r=0\), and \(Q=1\). In the 3-qubit W state each has \(r^2=1/9\) and \(Q=0.889\). If the global state is mixed, the deficit mixes entanglement and noise and cannot separate them: the radius measures entanglement only when the register is known, or guaranteed, to be pure. Reading \(r^2\) takes three measurement settings for the whole register (every qubit in \(X\), in \(Y\) and in \(Z\)), not three per qubit.

5.3 The radius under gates and algorithms
A single-qubit gate rotates the sphere and preserves the radius, also for mixed qubits. SWAP exchanges the radii of two qubits. CNOT, CZ, iSWAP, Toffoli and Fredkin can take a qubit of a product input to the centre (\(r=0\), from inputs of the type \(|{+}0\rangle\) or \(|{+}{+}\rangle\)) and can also bring it back to the surface; on computational-basis states they create no deficit, because they act as classical permutations (§97). text:
5.4 Definite weight: the radius from the Z basis
In a state of definite Hamming weight every local \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\) is zero, so \(r_q=|qg_Z^{(q)}|\) and the radius is read from \(Z\) shots alone. With the probability equation, the deficit becomes
\[
1-r^2=1-\left(\frac{m}{1000}\right)^2=4\,p_0\,(1-p_0):
\]
four times the binomial variance of the outcome, the same \(p_0(1-p_0)\) that governs the shot noise of Chapter 1. Figure 5.1 shows it on the milli-qang scale. The deficit is zero at the poles, largest on the equator and very sensitive near a pole: a qubit at 990 m-qg has a deficit of 0.02, and one at 800 m-qg, which is what 10 % of misplaced shots on a basis state gives, already reads 0.36.






Figure 5.1: The deficit of a definite-weight qubit against its milli-qang reading (bottom) and its probability (top). Near a pole, a few misplaced shots produce a large deficit.



This is where the symmetry filter (Chapters 20–21) and the radius meet. Under equal T1 on every qubit the filtered state is the noiseless pure state, so the filtered deficit is an exact entanglement measure. The predictions were committed before running (§98); on RBS circuits of 4 and 6 qubits:

On product states the filtered deficit is exactly 0 under all three noise models, while the raw read-out shows 0.60–0.95 on every excited qubit from decay alone: false entanglement. One prediction failed: the raw error was expected to be smaller at half filling, and it was larger (0.177 against 0.074), because the first-order cancellation holds only at exactly \(p=1/2\).
On noise models of real devices (three from IBM and two from IonQ, §100), the filter cut the error of the deficit 3.2–4.0× where the deficit is large, but it did not work as a test of “no entanglement”: on a product state it removed only 15–33 % of the false deficit. The cause is the one in Figure 5.1: errors inside the sector leave 10–21 % of misplaced shots, and near the pole that already reads as 0.36. A small deficit needs an echo calibration before it is interpreted.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.5 Direction and radius apart
The polar bias \(qg_Z=r\cos\theta\) mixes the direction of the vector with its length. The usual reading \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\) drifts towards the equator whenever noise shortens the vector. With the radius the two separate (§102):
\[
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2},\,qg_Z\right)=\arccos\frac{qg_Z}{r}.
\]
A state at \(30^\circ\) shortened to \(r=0.8\) by depolarizing noise has \(qg_Z=0.693\): \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) reads \(46.1^\circ\), and the separated angle reads the true \(30^\circ\). Figure 5.2 shows the effect for several radii: the naive angle flattens towards \(90^\circ\), and the separated one does not depend on \(r\).






Figure 5.2: The angle read against the true direction. The dashed curves are \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) for shortened vectors; the straight line is the angle separated from the radius, exact for any \(r\) under depolarizing noise.



The separation has a cost and does not always win. With the same total number of shots split over three bases:

Depolarizing: the separated angle is exact and \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) errs by up to 0.70 rad near the poles; with shots, the root-mean-square error drops 5.8×.
Dephasing: this is where it loses. Dephasing does not shorten \(qg_Z\), so \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) is exact, and the separated angle is pulled 0.03–0.12 rad towards the poles.
No noise: measuring three bases costs 1.6× in root-mean-square error.
Devices: on the IBM models the vector shrinks almost uniformly and the separated angle is 5–9× more accurate. On IonQ, \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) won at first, because the compiler had removed pairs of identical CX gates; in the native gate set the separated angle wins there too, 8.7–9.0× (§103).

The practical rule: if the measured radius is close to 1, use \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) with all shots in \(Z\); if it is clearly below 1 and the noise is not pure dephasing, use the separated angle. On the angular scale of Chapter 1 (Section 1.4), the example above is 83.3 qga true against 128.1 qga read.
The azimuthal phase does not depend on the radius. Since \(qg_X=r\sin\theta\cos\varphi\) and \(qg_Y=r\sin\theta\sin\varphi\), the ratio cancels \(r\) and \(\sin\theta\), and \(\varphi=\operatorname{atan2}(qg_Y,qg_X)\) is the same for the shortened vector. That holds whenever the noise shortens both transverse components equally: depolarizing noise, dephasing and T1 relaxation preserve the phase. A channel that treats \(X\) and \(Y\) differently shifts it: with a bit flip of probability 0.15, which keeps \(qg_X\) and shortens \(qg_Y\), a phase of 0.70 rad reads 0.53 rad.
Open proposals. The author’s working version adds a purity penalty \(\lambda_r(1-r^2)\) to the regularized energy of Chapter 1, damps the azimuthal part of the radiation function with \(r\) and, against noise-induced barren plateaus (Wang et al. 2021), proposes watching the radius layer by layer, discarding layers with \(r<0.3\) and compiling with minimum curvature \(\kappa_{qg}\), with a 35 to 60% reduction of exposure time. That noise produces plateaus is a known result; the three proposals and those figures have not been verified.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.6 Wave–particle duality and entropic uncertainty
The radius also orders a classical result of the foundations. The predictability \(P=|qg_Z|=|m|/1000\) measures how much is known about the path (particle) and the visibility \(V=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2}\) measures the contrast of the interference (wave). Their relation is exactly the radius (Greenberger and Yasin 1988; Englert 1996):
\[
P^2+V^2=r^2\le1 .
\]
The duality inequality is, in qg units, the statement that the state lies inside the sphere, and it is an equality for pure states (Figure 5.3). A state at \(60^\circ\) with \(r=0.9\) has \(P=0.45\), \(V=0.779\) and \(P^2+V^2=0.81\). It was checked on 2000 random states with a largest deviation of \(2.2\cdot10^{-16}\) (§127).






Figure 5.3: Wave–particle duality in qg units: each state is a point of the quarter disc, at distance \(r\) from the origin. Pure states lie on the arc \(r=1\).



The entropic version uses Chapter 1’s spread \(qg_S\) in two bases. The Maassen–Uffink relation, with the correction of Berta and co-workers for mixed states, says
\[
qg_S(Z)+qg_S(X)\ \ge\ 1+S(\rho),\qquad S(\rho)=H\!\left(\frac{1+r}{2}\right).
\]
For the state above the sum is 1.349 and the bound 1.286. The bound is tight: the state \(|0\rangle\) meets it with equality. That gives a practical warning. With plain (uncorrected) entropy estimates, a pure state seems to violate the relation in 93 % of runs at 100 shots, because the estimated entropy is biased downwards; with the Miller–Madow correction, in 37 %. A test of the bound needs corrected estimators or intervals, like those of Chapter 4.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.7 Estimating the radius from shots
Since \(r^2\) is a sum of squares, it inherits the bias of the quadratic estimators of Chapter 4 (Section 4.4): each axis adds \((1-qg^2)/N\), and an entangled state looks purer than it is. The exact correction \((N\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1)/(N-1)\) is applied axis by axis (radius2_estimate), and in a definite-weight state the \(Z\) axis is enough.

section: 5.8 The derived quantities inside the sphere
text:
5.8 The derived quantities inside the sphere
The derived quantities of Chapter 1 (Section 1.11) were defined on the reading, and they hold for a mixed qubit too. With the radius, four of them become tied to one another; Chapter 4 (Section 4.8) already covered how they are estimated.
The dissipative deficit is the square root of the surface deficit. Since \(qg_\tau=\sqrt{1-r^2}=2\sqrt{\det\rho}\), the one-tangle of Section 5.2 is \(qg_\tau^2\) and the global entanglement is \(Q=\frac1n\sum_q qg_{\tau,q}^2\). In a pure two-qubit register, the \(qg_\tau\) of either qubit is the concurrence (Coffman et al. 2000): it is 1 in the Bell state, and in the 3-qubit W state each qubit has \(qg_\tau=\sqrt{8/9}=0.943\). At definite weight the \(Z\) basis is enough: for \(0.6\,|01\rangle+0.8\,|10\rangle\) the readings are \(\mp280\) m-qg and \(qg_\tau=\sqrt{1-0.28^2}=0.96\), which is \(2|ab|\), the concurrence.
Duality with three terms. The definition gives an equality for any one-qubit state:
\[
P^2+V^2+qg_\tau^2=1 .
\]
What the inequality \(P^2+V^2\le1\) of Section 5.6 leaves unassigned is the dissipative deficit. When the qubit is part of a pure pair, \(qg_\tau\) is the concurrence and the equality is the complementarity relation of Jakob and Bergou (2010) between particle, wave and entanglement. The state at \(60^\circ\) with \(r=0.9\) splits into \(0.2025+0.6075+0.19\), with \(qg_\tau=0.436\). The warning of Section 5.2 applies: with a mixed global state the third term mixes entanglement and noise.
Shot noise splits in two. The same equality, written for the variance of one \(Z\) shot, is
\[
1-qg_Z^2=qg_\tau^2+V^2 :
\]
one part comes from the lack of purity and the other from coherence. At definite weight \(V=0\) and \(r=|qg_Z|\), so \(qg_\tau\) is the standard deviation of one shot and the other two quantities are functions of it: \(qg_{SNR}=r/qg_\tau\) and \(qg_\kappa=1/(\ln2\,qg_\tau^2)\). At 800 m-qg, \(qg_\tau=0.6\), \(qg_{SNR}=1.33\) and \(qg_\kappa=4.01\); at 990 m-qg, \(0.141\), \(7.02\) and \(72.5\).
The shots for a sign with a shortened vector. \(qg_{SNR}\) is computed from the reading, and the reading is \(r\cos\theta\): noise that shortens the vector lowers the signal and raises the noise at once,
\[
N_\text{sign}=z^2\,\frac{1-r^2\cos^2\theta}{r^2\cos^2\theta}.
\]
At \(60^\circ\) and 3σ that is 27 shots with \(r=1\), 36 with \(r=0.9\), 48 with \(r=0.8\) and 135 with \(r=0.5\). The shot budget is planned with the radius expected on the device, not with the ideal state.
The geodesic distance sees only part of the shortening. \(qg_L\) compares two \(Z\) readings through the qang angle \(\arccos qg_Z\), not through the Bloch polar angle. In the example of Section 5.5, the state at \(30^\circ\) and the same state shortened to \(r=0.8\) are \(qg_L=0.141\) rad (22.4 qga) apart. Their distance as quantum states is the Bures angle, \(\arccos\sqrt F=0.322\) rad with \(F=(1+r)/2=0.9\), and since a measurement cannot increase distinguishability (Nielsen and Chuang 2010), \(qg_L\) is always a lower bound: here it sees 44%. The two coincide if the state is at a pole, and on the equator \(qg_L=0\) for any radius. With the reference angle known, \(\widehat{qg}_L\) has standard deviation \(1/(2\sqrt N)\), and seeing that shortening at 3σ takes \(N=(z/2qg_L)^2=114\) shots in \(Z\). Hence the decision: a calibration state near a pole reveals the shortening without measuring three bases; near the equator all three are needed.
One basis against three, in shots. Reading the deficit of a definite-weight state in \(Z\) alone saves two settings and shots as well. With 300 shots in total and a qubit at 800 m-qg, the standard error of \(\hat r^{\,2}\) is 0.055 with all of them in \(Z\) and 0.098 split over three bases (exact binomial sums): the variance is 3.1 times larger, and at least 3 times in the cases checked (from 0 to 990 m-qg). The gain belongs to the weight symmetry, which cancels \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\); the probability equation turns it into a reading.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.11 Summary

For a mixed state, Chapter 1’s probability equation still holds with \(qg_Z=r\cos\theta\); the local radius \(r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2=2\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2-1\) is the missing reading.
If the register is pure, the deficit \(1-r^2\) is the one-tangle and its mean is the Meyer–Wallach measure; with a mixed global state, it mixes entanglement and noise.
At definite weight, \(1-r^2=4p_0(1-p_0)\) is read in \(Z\) alone, and with the filter under equal T1 it is exact; near a pole a few misplaced shots inflate it, and on devices a small deficit needs calibration.
\(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z/r)\) separates direction from purity: it wins under depolarizing noise and loses under pure dephasing.
Wave–particle duality is \(P^2+V^2=r^2\), and entropic uncertainty bounds \(qg_S(Z)+qg_S(X)\) by \(1+S(\rho)\).
Of the derived quantities: \(P^2+V^2+qg_\tau^2=1\), and \(qg_\tau\) is the concurrence of a pure pair; at definite weight \(qg_\tau\) is the standard deviation of one shot, with \(qg_{SNR}=r/qg_\tau\) and \(qg_\kappa=1/(\ln2\,qg_\tau^2)\); \(qg_L\) in \(Z\) is a lower bound of the Bures angle, blind on the equator.

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.1 The polarized photon as a qubit
Actualizado: 17 de noviembre de 2026 · Updated: November 17, 2026
The polarization of a photon is a qubit, and classical polarization optics is, unchanged, the physics of a qubit written with other names. Chapters 1 to 5 built that physics from four pieces: the probability equation \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\) and its reading \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\) (Chapter 1), the gate rule and the transition probability between two qg vectors (Chapters 2 and 3), the statistics of counts (Chapter 4) and the local radius that separates direction from purity (Chapter 5). This chapter adds no new piece: it shows that the optics laboratory already uses all of them.
The central idea is that a polarizer is a two-outcome measurement, pass or block, and its transmission is exactly the probability \(p_0\) of the qang equation. From there follow, in this order, Malus’s law (Section 6.2), the Stokes parameters (Section 6.3), the degree of polarization (Section 6.4), Mueller calculus (Section 6.5) and photon-counting polarimetry (Section 6.6), all in qg and in milli-qang (§83). Each identity is derived here step by step; the chapter closes with the balance of what changes and what does not when the qang scale is used (Section 6.8).
Intuition. A plane wave travelling in a fixed direction has its electric field in the transverse plane, and that plane has two dimensions. Two complex amplitudes, one per transverse direction, describe the polarization completely: that is the definition of a qubit.
Formalism. In the horizontal–vertical basis, the Jones vector is
\[
|E\rangle=E_H|H\rangle+E_V|V\rangle,\qquad |H\rangle\equiv|0\rangle,\quad |V\rangle\equiv|1\rangle,
\]
normalized to \(\langle E|E\rangle=1\) for one photon. Real light fluctuates, and what is measured are quadratic averages of the field. Those averages form the coherence matrix, which, normalized by the intensity, is the density operator of the earlier chapters:
\[
\rho=\frac{\langle\,|E\rangle\langle E|\,\rangle}{\operatorname{Tr}\langle\,|E\rangle\langle E|\,\rangle}
=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb 1+qg_X\,\sigma_x+qg_Y\,\sigma_y+qg_Z\,\sigma_z\right)
=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb 1+\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right),
\]
with \(\mathbf r=(qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\) the qg vector of the light and \(qg_P=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_P)\), as in Chapter 5 (Section 5.1).
Angle doubling. Light linearly polarized at an angle \(\alpha\) from the horizontal is \(|\alpha\rangle=\cos\alpha\,|H\rangle+\sin\alpha\,|V\rangle\). Its qg values are
\[
qg_Z=\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha=\cos2\alpha,\qquad qg_X=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=\sin2\alpha,\qquad qg_Y=0 .
\]
The state lies on the meridian \(qg_Y=0\) of the sphere, at polar angle \(\theta=2\alpha\): the qang angle is twice the physical angle. That is why two orthogonal polarizations, H and V, \(90^\circ\) apart in the laboratory, are opposite points of the sphere, \(180^\circ\) apart, that is, 500 qga (Figure 6.1). The doubling is not a convention: rotating a polarizer by \(180^\circ\) leaves it unchanged, while a point on the sphere needs \(360^\circ\) to return to its place.

section: 6.2 Malus’s law as a probability equation
text:
6.2 Malus’s law as a probability equation

6.2.1 Linearly polarized light
An ideal polarizer oriented at \(\vartheta\) passes the component of the field along its axis and absorbs the perpendicular one. As an operator it is the projector \(\Pi_\vartheta=|\vartheta\rangle\langle\vartheta|\), with \(\Pi_\vartheta^2=\Pi_\vartheta\): it is not a gate, it is a measurement with two outcomes. For linear light at \(\alpha\) and \(\Delta=\vartheta-\alpha\), the transmitted fraction is
\[
p_0=\lVert\Pi_\vartheta|\alpha\rangle\rVert^2=\lvert\langle\vartheta|\alpha\rangle\rvert^2
=\left(\cos\vartheta\cos\alpha+\sin\vartheta\sin\alpha\right)^2=\cos^2\Delta .
\]
This is Malus’s law. For an intense beam it is a fraction of intensity, \(I=I_0\cos^2\Delta\); for a single photon it is a probability. The comparison with the Born rule of Chapter 1, \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\), is immediate: \(\theta=2\Delta\), and the milli-qang reading is
\[
m=1000\,qg_Z=1000\cos2\Delta .
\]
An analyzer turned \(30^\circ\) from the light transmits \(p_0=0.75\): it is the state of \(\theta=60^\circ\) (166.7 qga) and \(+500\) m-qg of the qang circle of Chapter 1 (Figure 1.1). Here it is worth recalling the distinction of Chapter 1: the \(60^\circ\) are an angle and are expressed in qga; the \(+500\) is a reading, linear in the probability, and is expressed in m-qg.


6.2.2 Light of any polarization
For pure or partially polarized light the transmission is \(p_0=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\Pi_\vartheta)\). The projector has the same form as \(\rho\), with the qg vector of the state that the analyzer lets through,
\[
\Pi_\vartheta=\frac12\left(\mathbb 1+\mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right),\qquad
\mathbf a=(\sin2\vartheta,\,0,\,\cos2\vartheta),
\]
and with \(\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_i\sigma_j)=2\delta_{ij}\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_i=0\) one gets
\[
p_0=\frac14\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(\mathbb 1+\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)(\mathbb 1+\mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)\right]
=\frac{1+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a}{2}
=\frac{1+qg_Z\cos2\vartheta+qg_X\sin2\vartheta}{2}.
\tag{6.1}\]
It is the transition probability of Chapter 3 between two qg vectors (Section 3.4), and its milli-qang reading is \(m=1000\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a\). The circular component \(qg_Y\) does not appear: a linear polarizer, at any orientation, is blind to it.
Maximum, minimum and contrast. With \(P_{\text{lin}}=\sqrt{qg_Z^2+qg_X^2}\) and \(\tan2\psi=qg_X/qg_Z\), the scalar product is \(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a=P_{\text{lin}}\cos(2\vartheta-2\psi)\), so that
\[
p_0^{\max}=\frac{1+P_{\text{lin}}}{2}\ \text{at}\ \vartheta=\psi,\qquad
p_0^{\min}=\frac{1-P_{\text{lin}}}{2}\ \text{at}\ \vartheta=\psi+90^\circ,\qquad
p_0^{\max}-p_0^{\min}=P_{\text{lin}} .
\]
The contrast of the curve as the polarizer turns measures the linear part of the polarization, not the total degree of polarization; the two coincide only if \(qg_Y=0\).
Figure 6.2 shows four cases: H light (\(\cos^2\vartheta\)), D light (the same curve shifted by \(45^\circ\)), unpolarized light (always \(\tfrac12\), that is, 0 m-qg) and partially polarized light with \(qg_Z=0.6\) and \(qg_X=0.3\). The last one transmits 0.80 at \(0^\circ\), a maximum of 0.835 at \(13.3^\circ\) and a minimum of 0.165 at \(103.3^\circ\). Since it has no circular component, the difference between maximum and minimum, 0.671, is its degree of polarization. If \(qg_Y=0.4\) is added to that same light, the curve does not change and the contrast stays at 0.671, but the degree of polarization rises to 0.781: seeing it takes a quarter-wave plate in front of the polarizer (Section 6.5).






Figure 6.2: Malus’s law as a probability equation: transmission of a linear polarizer against its angle, with its milli-qang reading on the right.

6.3 The Stokes parameters are qg values

6.3.1 Operational definition
Stokes defined his four parameters as sums and differences of intensities behind six analyzers:
\[
S_0=I_H+I_V,\qquad S_1=I_H-I_V,\qquad S_2=I_D-I_A,\qquad S_3=I_R-I_L .
\]
Dividing by \(S_0\) turns each intensity into a probability, and each difference into a \(2p_0-1\) in its own basis. With \(|H\rangle=|0\rangle\) and \(|V\rangle=|1\rangle\), the normalized Stokes parameters are then the three qg values, and the Poincaré sphere is the Bloch sphere:

The first row is the probability equation of Chapter 1. The second is Equation 6.1 evaluated at \(\vartheta=\pm45^\circ\): \(p_D-p_A=qg_X\). The third needs the circular basis, and the convention for right circular changes from one text to another; here \(|R\rangle=(|H\rangle+i|V\rangle)/\sqrt2\), so that \(S_3>0\) means \(qg_Y>0\) (the library accepts the opposite convention with circular_sign=-1). Since each parameter is \(2p_0-1\) in its own basis, each is expressed in milli-qang with the equation of Chapter 1.


6.3.2 The polarization ellipse
The tip of the electric field traces an ellipse, with orientation \(\psi\) of its major axis and ellipticity \(\chi\) (\(\tan\chi\) is the ratio of the semi-axes). In terms of those two angles, the qg vector is
\[
qg_Z=P\cos2\chi\cos2\psi,\qquad qg_X=P\cos2\chi\sin2\psi,\qquad qg_Y=P\sin2\chi ,
\]
with \(P\) the length of the vector (Section 6.4). Inverting,
\[
\psi=\tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(qg_X,qg_Z),\qquad \chi=\tfrac12\arcsin\frac{qg_Y}{P} .
\]
The ellipse is read with the angles of the qg vector divided by two: it is the doubling of Section 6.1 in both directions. For the partially polarized light of the example, \(\psi=13.3^\circ\), the angle where Figure 6.2 has its maximum, and \(\chi=0\); with \(qg_Y=0.4\) added, \(\chi=15.4^\circ\).
A remark on the two spheres. They are the same, but each tradition picks a different pole: optics puts the circular polarizations at the poles and measures \(2\chi\) as latitude; qang puts at the poles the two outcomes of the measurement, H and V. The qang polar angle of pure light is therefore \(\cos\theta=\cos2\chi\cos2\psi\), and it equals \(2\psi\) only for linear light.

text:
6.4 Degree of polarization and purity

6.4.1 The degree of polarization is the radius
Partially polarized light is a mixed state. Its degree of polarization is the length of the qg vector, the radius of Chapter 5 (Section 5.1):
\[
P=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2}=r,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=\frac{1+P^2}{2}.
\]
The second equality follows from \((\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2=P^2\,\mathbb 1\):
\[
\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=\frac14\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\mathbb 1+2\,\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma+P^2\,\mathbb 1\right]
=\frac{2+2P^2}{4}.
\]
The eigenvalues of \(\rho\) are \((1\pm P)/2\), and with \(\mathbf n=\mathbf r/P\) the spectral decomposition rearranges as
\[
\rho=P\,\frac{\mathbb 1+\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma}{2}+(1-P)\,\frac{\mathbb 1}{2} :
\]
a fraction \(P\) of fully polarized light in direction \(\mathbf n\) and a fraction \(1-P\) of unpolarized light. It is the classical decomposition of optics, and here it is the reading of \(r\) as a radius: unpolarized light is at the center of the sphere, fully polarized light on its surface.


6.4.2 The depolarizer separates direction and radius
An ideal depolarizer has Mueller matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,d,d,d)\): it shortens the vector by a factor \(d\) and does not change its direction. It is the case in which Chapter 5 separates direction and radius (Section 5.5): with \(d=0.7\), the light of the example goes from \(P=0.671\) to \(P=0.470\), and the orientation of its ellipse stays at \(13.3^\circ\). The polar bias, in contrast, falls from 0.60 to 0.42, and the naive reading \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) goes from \(53.1^\circ\) to \(65.2^\circ\): a false broadening of \(12^\circ\) attributable to noise. The separated angle \(\arccos(qg_Z/P)=26.57^\circ\) (73.8 qga on the scale of Chapter 1) does not change.

6.4.3 Complementarity
The predictability in the H/V basis, \(P_Z=\lvert qg_Z\rvert\), says how much can be anticipated about whether the photon will pass a horizontal polarizer. The fringe visibility in the transverse bases, \(V=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2}\), says how much coherence is left between H and V. By the definition of \(P\), they satisfy exactly
\[
P_Z^2+V^2=P^2\le1 .
\]
The Greenberger–Yasin–Englert inequality is here the condition that the Stokes vector lie inside the Poincaré sphere, with equality for fully polarized light.
The entropic version uses the measurement entropy \(qg_S\) of Chapter 1. The H/V and R/L bases are mutually unbiased, so the Maassen–Uffink bound is 1 bit; for a mixed state the entropy of the state itself is added (Berta et al. 2010), which by the eigenvalues \((1\pm P)/2\) is \(S(\rho)=H\big((1+P)/2\big)\):
\[
qg_S(Z)+qg_S(Y)\ \ge\ 1+H\!\left(\frac{1+P}{2}\right).
\]
It is the duality of Chapter 5 (Section 5.6) read in polarimetry: the less polarized the light, the more uncertain both analyzers are at once.

text:
6.5 Lossless elements: the Mueller matrix is the gate rule

6.5.1 From Jones to Mueller
A linear optical element acts on the Jones vector with a matrix \(J\), and therefore on the coherence matrix as \(\rho\mapsto J\rho J^\dagger\). Writing \(\rho\) in the basis \((\mathbb 1,\sigma_z,\sigma_x,\sigma_y)\), which is the Stokes order \((S_0,S_1,S_2,S_3)\), the action on the four parameters is the Mueller matrix
\[
M_{\mu\nu}=\frac12\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma_\mu\,J\,\sigma_\nu\,J^\dagger\right).
\]
In that order, it is the Pauli transfer matrix of quantum information. For a lossless element \(J=U\) is unitary, the first row and first column are \((1,0,0,0)\) and the remaining block gives exactly the qang gate rule:
\[
qg'_P=qg_{U^\dagger P U}.
\]


6.5.2 Wave plates are rotations of the sphere
A wave plate with retardance \(\delta\) and fast axis at an angle \(\varphi\) delays one linear component with respect to the perpendicular one. Up to a global phase, its Jones matrix is
\[
U(\delta,\varphi)=\exp\!\left(-\,i\,\frac{\delta}{2}\,\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right),\qquad
\mathbf n=(\sin2\varphi,\,0,\,\cos2\varphi),
\]
and therefore it rotates the qg vector by an angle \(\delta\) about the axis \(\mathbf n\), which is the point of the sphere corresponding to the linear polarization of the fast axis. Wave plates are one-qubit gates, and Chapter 2 applies as it stands (Section 2.3):

The half-wave plate with its axis at \(22.5^\circ\) takes H to D because it rotates the physical polarization by \(45^\circ\) and the point of the sphere by \(90^\circ\). The quarter-wave plate at \(45^\circ\) turns by \(90^\circ\) about the \(qg_X\) axis and takes the H pole to the circular axis; the sign, \(qg_Y=-1\), depends on the convention of Section 6.3.1. That same plate, placed in front of a polarizer, takes the circular axis to the H/V pole: it is what allows \(qg_Y\) to be measured with a linear analyzer and completes the third row of Table 6.1.
The polarizer, in contrast, is not unitary. Its Mueller matrix is
\[
M_{\text{pol}}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\\ \mathbf a&\mathbf a\,\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix},
\]
with \(\mathbf a\) in the order \((Z,X,Y)\): the transmitted intensity is Equation 6.1 and the outgoing light is fully polarized along \(\mathbf a\), whatever came in. It is the projection postulate written in Stokes parameters. All these identities are checked numerically in tests/test_polarization.py and in tools/verify_cap06_expansion.py.

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.6 Photon-counting polarimetry

6.6.1 One qg value per basis
With weak or single-photon sources, the Stokes parameters are estimated by counting: \(n_H,n_V\) in the H/V basis, \(n_D,n_A\) in the diagonal one and \(n_R,n_L\) in the circular one. Each pair is a binomial experiment and gives a qg value with its interval, just like a one-qubit measurement (Chapter 4):
\[
\widehat{qg}_Z=\frac{n_H-n_V}{n_H+n_V},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\big(\widehat{qg}_Z\big)=\frac{1-qg_Z^2}{N},
\]
and the same for the other two bases. With 1000 photons per basis and counts \((800,200)\), \((650,350)\) and \((500,500)\):
\[
qg_Z=0.599\ [0.548;\,0.647],\quad qg_X=0.299\ [0.240;\,0.358],\quad qg_Y=0.000\ [-0.062;\,0.062],
\]
95 % Bayes–Haar intervals. In milli-qang, \(qg_Z\) is \(+599\) m-qg with a resolution of \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N=25\) m-qg.


6.6.2 The bias of the degree of polarization
The degree of polarization needs more care. \(P\) is the root of a sum of squares, and the square of an unbiased estimator is not unbiased. From \(E[\hat q^{\,2}]=q^2+\operatorname{Var}(\hat q)\),
\[
E\big[\widehat{qg}^{\,2}\big]=qg^2+\frac{1-qg^2}{N},
\]
which is the bias of Chapter 4 (Section 4.4), and the estimator that cancels it is \((N\,\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1)/(N-1)\). The bias is largest where it matters most: at \(qg=0\). With few photons, unpolarized light looks polarized.
For unpolarized light the effect is computed in closed form. Each \(\widehat{qg}\) is approximately normal with zero mean and variance \(1/N\), so that \(\hat P\sqrt N\) is the length of a three-component Gaussian vector and follows the Maxwell distribution:
\[
E\big[\hat P\big]\approx\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi N}}\approx\frac{1.6}{\sqrt N}.
\]
Figure 6.3 quantifies it with a simulation from this chapter (4000 repetitions per point). With unpolarized light, the plug-in estimator gives on average \(\hat P\approx0.50\) with 10 photons per basis, \(0.16\) with 100 and \(0.05\) with 1000, which are the values of the formula. Using the unbiased squares lowers it about threefold (\(\approx0.18\), \(0.055\) and \(0.017\)), but does not cancel it: the root and the clipping at zero leave a residual bias. With light of \(P=0.5\), the plug-in estimator overestimates with few photons and the unbiased one slightly underestimates; from about 200 photons per basis the two agree with the true value.






Figure 6.3: Bias of the degree of polarization estimated by counting, against the photons per basis. Solid lines: plug-in estimator; dashed: with the unbiased squares of Chapter 4. The horizontal dotted lines mark the true value.



The practical consequence: to claim that a source is polarized with few photons, one needs an interval for \(P\) or a threshold calibrated with unpolarized light, not the point value. The Maxwell formula gives the scale of that threshold: a \(\hat P\) of order \(1.6/\sqrt N\) is what a source with no polarization at all delivers.


6.6.3 Open proposals
The author’s working version carries the regularized energy of Chapter 1 over to programmable optics, with a penalty \(\lambda_r(1-P^2)\) that punishes the depolarization of the interferometer, and a radiation function whose azimuthal part is attenuated with \(P\). As in the previous chapters, the penalties are not defined and neither proposal has been verified.

6.9 In code
import math
import numpy as np
from qang import polarization as pz

# --- Malus's law: transmission of a linear polarizer for any light
light = {"Z": 0.6, "X": 0.3, "Y": 0.0}
pz.malus_intensity(light, 0.0)                    # 0.80: transmission at 0°
pz.malus_intensity(light, math.radians(13.28))    # 0.835: the maximum, at the ellipse orientation

# --- Wave plates: one-qubit gates on the Jones vector
H = np.array([1, 0])
pz.jones_to_qg(pz.half_wave_plate(math.radians(22.5)) @ H)   # {'X': 1.0, ...}: H → D
pz.jones_to_qg(pz.quarter_wave_plate(math.radians(45)) @ H)  # {'Y': -1.0, ...}: H → circular

# --- From Jones to Mueller: the 3×3 block is the rotation by δ about (sin 2φ, 0, cos 2φ)
M = pz.mueller_from_jones(pz.wave_plate(math.pi / 2, math.radians(45)))   # order (S0, S1, S2, S3)

# --- Depolarizer: shortens the vector without turning it
S = pz.depolarizer(0.7) @ pz.qg_to_stokes(light)
pz.degree_of_polarization(S)                      # 0.470 (before 0.671)
pz.stokes_to_qg(S)                                # {'X': 0.21, 'Y': 0.0, 'Z': 0.42}

# --- Photon-counting polarimetry: three bases, Bayes–Haar intervals
c = pz.qg_from_counts(800, 200, 650, 350, 500, 500, method="bayes")
c["Z"], c["X"], c["P"]                            # 0.6, 0.3, 0.671 and the intervals in c["intervals"]
The figures are generated with tools/make_cap06_figures.py. The depolarizer and complementarity examples are checked with tools/verify_cap06.py, and the derivations of this chapter (the retarder as a rotation, the extremes of Malus’s law, the polarizer as a projector, the bias of the square and the Maxwell mean) with tools/verify_cap06_expansion.py.

6.10 Summary and link to Chapter 7

A polarized photon is a qubit: the Jones vector is the state, the normalized coherence matrix is \(\rho\), and linear polarization at \(\alpha\) lies at qang angle \(\theta=2\alpha\).
A polarizer is a two-outcome measurement: its transmission is \(p_0=\cos^2\Delta\), the probability equation of Chapter 1 with \(\theta=2\Delta\).
For any light, Malus’s law is the transition probability \((1+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a)/2\) between the light and the analyzer; its reading is \(1000\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a\) m-qg, and the contrast as the polarizer turns is the linear part \(\sqrt{qg_Z^2+qg_X^2}\).
The normalized Stokes parameters are \(qg_Z\), \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\); the ellipse is read with half the angles of the qg vector.
The degree of polarization is the radius of Chapter 5; a depolarizer shortens it without turning the ellipse.
Wave plates are gates: the lossless Mueller matrix is the rule \(qg'_P=qg_{U^\dagger PU}\), and a retarder rotates the qg vector by an angle equal to its retardance about the point of its fast axis.
By photon counting, each parameter has its interval; the degree of polarization is biased upward with few photons, unpolarized light gives \(\hat P\approx1.6/\sqrt N\), and the unbiased squares reduce that bias about threefold without eliminating it.

Toward Chapter 7. This whole chapter dealt with probabilities: what a polarizer lets through. But wave plates move the state over the sphere, and a state that runs along a closed path returns to the same point with something that no measurement in a single basis records: a phase. If a sequence of plates takes the polarization around a triangle H → D → R → H, the light exits with the same polarization and with a phase that depends only on the area enclosed on the Poincaré sphere. It is the Pancharatnam phase, and its general version is the Berry phase. Chapter 7 (?sec-ch07) computes it with Stokes’s theorem on the same sphere that here served to read the Stokes parameters, and shows how an interferometer turns it into a probability, that is, again into a qang reading.

title: Chapter 7 — Quantum Angular Networks (QAN), Mutual Information in qang Space and Regularized Inversion (IQAN)
text:
7.1 QAN: the network as a qga → qg map
Updated: November 15, 2026
A QAN is a differentiable map \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^P_{\text{qga}}\to[-1,1]^n\times[-1,1]^{n\times n}\) that sends angular parameters (scale qga, \(\theta=2\pi\,\alpha/1000\)) to projective readings in a single \(Z\) basis. Canonical layer: \[|\psi(\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma)\rangle=\Big[\bigotimes_q R_Y(\gamma_q)\Big]\Big[\prod_{(p,q)\in E}R_{ZZ}(\beta_{pq})\Big]\Big[\bigotimes_q R_Y(\alpha_q)\Big]|0\rangle^{\otimes n},\qquad \alpha,\beta,\gamma\ \text{in qga}.\] Reading: \(qg_Z^{(q)}=\langle Z_q\rangle\), \(qg_{ZZ}^{(pq)}=\langle Z_pZ_q\rangle\), both from the same histogram \(|\psi|^2\). Every \(qg_Z^{(q)}\) and every pairwise correlator \(qg_{ZZ}^{(pq)}\) comes from one histogram; no ancilla, no extra two-qubit gate, no basis change. \(R_{ZZ}\) has period \(500\) qga in the reading: \(R_{ZZ}(\beta+500)=-i\,Z\!\otimes\!Z\,R_{ZZ}(\beta)\) and the factor \(Z\!\otimes\!Z\) is absorbed as a virtual \(R_Z(\pi)\) (\(\gamma\to-\gamma\)), invisible in \(|\psi|^2\) (Ch. 2, exact).

title: Chapter 7 — Quantum Angular Networks (QAN), Mutual Information in qang Space and Regularized Inversion (IQAN)
text:
7.2 MI in qang space
The joint \(Z\) distribution of a pair is the exact inversion of its Pauli expansion: \[p_{ab}(s,t)=\tfrac14\big(1+s\,qg_Z^{(a)}+t\,qg_Z^{(b)}+st\,qg_{ZZ}^{(ab)}\big),\quad s,t\in\{+1,-1\}.\] Mutual information (bits): \[I_Z(a;b)=qg_S^{(a)}+qg_S^{(b)}-H(p_{ab}),\qquad qg_S=H\!\big(\tfrac{1+qg_Z}{2}\big),\qquad 0\le I_Z\le\min\big(qg_S^{(a)},qg_S^{(b)}\big)\le1.\] Three qang numbers (\(qg_Z^{(a)},qg_Z^{(b)},qg_{ZZ}^{(ab)}\)) determine \(I_Z\). Limit (THEORY_CORE §2.4, against): \(I_Z\) depends on the \(Z\) basis and is not an entanglement measure (a rotated product state can give \(I_Z=0\) with maximal entanglement and vice versa). Its legitimate use is classical: deciding which pairs are worth coupling in a given layer and how many shots it costs to estimate them.
Shot budget (delta method, asymptotically exact): with \(\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\top\) and \(g=\partial I_Z/\partial p\), \[\mathrm{Var}(\hat I_Z)\simeq\frac{g^\top\Sigma g}{N},\qquad N^\star(\sigma_I)=\frac{g^\top\Sigma g}{\sigma_I^2}.\] At \(I_Z=0\) the gradient \(g\) vanishes and the estimator is biased at second order (\(\mathbb E[\hat I_Z]\approx 1/(2N\ln2)\) bits for the \(2\times2\) table, Miller–Madow): use a threshold \(\tau>1/(2N\ln 2)\) in every pruning. The shot cost is planned by the delta method with \(g\) obtained by automatic differentiation.

title: Chapter 7 — Quantum Angular Networks (QAN), Mutual Information in qang Space and Regularized Inversion (IQAN)
text:
7.3 IQAN: regularized inversion in angle
Given a target \((qg_Z^{\star},I^{\star})\), IQAN solves \[\min_{\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma\in\text{qga}}\ \mathcal L=\big\|qg_Z-qg_Z^{\star}\big\|_2^2+\lambda\sum_{(p,q)\in E}\big(I_Z^{(pq)}-I^{\star}_{pq}\big)^2+\mu\sum_{(p,q)\in E}\Big(\frac{\beta_{pq}}{500}\Big)^2 .\] The descent is Euclidean in angle (qga): by THEORY_CORE §2.1 it is first-order equivalent to the step damped by \(qg_\kappa\) in \(qg_Z\) and avoids the polar divergence of flat descent in \(qg_Z\) (0/20, against). The \(\mu\) term is minimum-area compilation: it penalizes \(|\beta|\) and, because of the 500 qga period, the minimum of a maximal entangler falls at \(\beta=250\) qga. Learning rate: \(\eta_{\text{qga}}=\eta_{\text{rad}}\,(1000/2\pi)^2\) (exact rescaling, no effect on barren plateaus, §2.1).

title: Chapter 8 — Coupling QAN to Probability Distributions: qg Moments, k-Local Truncation, Divergences and Shot Budget
text:
8.1 Every readout distribution is a vector of qg moments
Updated: November 15, 2026
For \(n\) qubits read in \(Z\), \(p(x)=|\langle x|\psi\rangle|^2\) admits the exact Walsh–Hadamard expansion in qang moments: \[p(x)=2^{-n}\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}qg_{Z_S}\,\chi_S(x),\qquad qg_{Z_S}=\langle Z_S\rangle=\sum_x p(x)\chi_S(x),\quad \chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}z_i(x),\ z_i\in\{\pm1\}.\] \(qg_{Z_\emptyset}=1\); \(|S|=1\) are the \(qg_Z^{(q)}\) of Ch. 1; \(|S|=2\) the \(qg_{ZZ}^{(pq)}\) of Ch. 7. Parseval: \(\|p-r\|_2^2=2^{-n}\sum_S(\Delta qg_{Z_S})^2\). Convention: qubit \(q\leftrightarrow\) bit \(n-1-q\) of \(x\) and of \(S\) (big-endian), identical to qang.qan. The \(Z\)-readout distribution is exactly the Walsh transform of its qang moments; first- and second-order moments are the \(qg_Z\) and \(qg_{ZZ}\) of Chapters 1 and 7. Parseval links the \(L_2\) error in \(p\) to the \(L_2\) error in the moments (exact).

title: Chapter 8 — Coupling QAN to Probability Distributions: qg Moments, k-Local Truncation, Divergences and Shot Budget
text:
8.2 k-local truncation and shot bound
Keeping the \(M_k=\sum_{j\le k}\binom nj\) moments of order \(\le k\) gives the \(L_2\) projection \(p_{(k)}\) (it can be negative if \(k<n\): it is an estimator, not a distribution). Sampling-error bound (Cauchy–Schwarz + Parseval, exact): \[\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{TV}(\hat p,p)\big]\le\tfrac12\sqrt{M/N},\qquad M=\begin{cases}2^n-1&\text{full histogram}\\ M_k&\text{moments}\le k\end{cases}\] Since each \(\hat{qg}_{Z_S}\) has \(\mathrm{Var}\le1/N\) uniformly in \(S\), the budget for TV \(\le\varepsilon\) is \(N^\star=M/(4\varepsilon^2)\): the saving against the histogram is exactly \(1-M_k/(2^n-1)\) and it is paid for with the truncation bias \(\mathrm{TV}(p_{(k)},p)\), which does depend on the state (in verify_cap08.py §2: \(0.126\) for a random 4-qubit QAN layer; mixed). Keeping only \(k\)-local moments trades an exact, state-independent shot saving for a state-dependent truncation bias; both are reported, neither is hidden (exact bound, mixed bias).

text:
8.3 Divergences in qg coordinates
\[D(qg_Z\|qg_Z')=\sum_{s=\pm}\tfrac{1+s\,qg_Z}{2}\log_2\frac{1+s\,qg_Z}{1+s\,qg_Z'}\ \text{[bit]},\qquad H^2(qg_Z,qg_Z')=1-\sqrt{p_0p_0'}-\sqrt{p_1p_1'}=1-\cos qg_L,\] with \(qg_L=|\theta-\theta'|/2\) the geodesic distance of Ch. 1 (common meridian, exact). In m-qg reading both are evaluated at \(m/1000\); the Fisher metric of \(D\) in \(qg_Z\) is \(qg_\kappa=1/(\ln2(1-qg_Z^2))\) (Ch. 1), which repeats the prohibition of flat descent in \(qg_Z\) (THEORY_CORE §2.1): every optimization of \(D\) or \(H^2\) in this chapter is done in qga.

text:
8.4 Haar prior and Bayesian reading
\(p_0\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\Leftrightarrow qg_Z\sim\mathcal U[-1,1]\) (Ch. 4). Posterior after \(N\) shots with \(k_0\) zeros: \(\mathrm{Beta}(1+k_0,\,1+N-k_0)\), \[\mathbb E[qg_Z]=\frac{2(1+k_0)}{N+2}-1,\qquad \mathrm{Var}[qg_Z]=\frac{4(1+k_0)(1+N-k_0)}{(N+2)^2(N+3)}.\] At the equator (\(k_0=N/2\)): \(\sigma=1000/\sqrt{N+3}\) m-qg (\(31.58\) m-qg at \(N=1000\)), with no coverage collapse at the poles (exact).

title: Chapter 9 — Fisher Information in qga: Z Readout versus Fubini–Study, Regularized Natural Gradient and Barren Plateaus
text:
9.1 Classical Fisher information of the Z readout in qga
Updated: November 15, 2026
For \(\theta=2\pi\alpha/1000\) and \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\): \[I_F(\alpha)=\frac{(\partial_\alpha p_0)^2}{p_0(1-p_0)}=\Big(\frac{2\pi}{1000}\Big)^2=4\pi^2\cdot10^{-6}\ \text{qga}^{-2}\quad\forall\alpha,\qquad \sigma_{\text{qga}}(N)=\frac{159.15}{\sqrt N}\ \text{qga}.\] It is uniform in the angle; in the readout coordinate, \(I_F(qg_Z)=1/(1-qg_Z^2)\) diverges at the poles and \(qg_\kappa=I_F/\ln2\) (Ch. 1). For the \(P\) parameters of a QAN, the classical Fisher matrix of the Z readout is \[F_{ij}=\sum_x\frac{\partial_ip(x)\,\partial_jp(x)}{p(x)},\] computable from the histogram alone and \(2P\) parameter-shift circuits, without an ancilla (exact). The \(Z\)-readout Fisher information is constant in qga and divergent in \(qg_Z\); the full classical Fisher matrix of a QAN needs only histograms and \(2P\) parameter-shift circuits.

section: 9.2 Fubini–Study metric and the Fisher bound by the metric
text:
9.2 Fubini–Study metric and the Fisher bound by the metric
\[g_{ij}=\mathrm{Re}\big[\langle\partial_i\psi|\partial_j\psi\rangle-\langle\partial_i\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\partial_j\psi\rangle\big],\qquad \text{QFI}=4g,\qquad F_Z\preceq4g,\] with equality for \(P=1\) and an \(R_Y\) rotation read in \(Z\) (meridian, exact). Estimating \(g\) on hardware requires \(P(P+1)/2+P\) overlaps with a Hadamard test (1 ancilla, controlled gates); \(F_Z\) requires \(2P\) circuits and 0 ancillas. With \(P=8\): 44 versus 16 circuits.

text:
9.3 Regularized natural gradient in qga
\[\boldsymbol\alpha\leftarrow\boldsymbol\alpha-\eta\,(F_Z+\lambda I)^{-1}\nabla_{\!\boldsymbol\alpha}\mathcal L,\qquad\lambda>0\ \text{mandatory}\ (F_Z\ \text{is singular at the poles and in directions not observable in }Z).\] For \(P=1\) this reproduces exactly the step damped by \(qg_\kappa\) and the Euclidean descent in \(\theta\) (THEORY_CORE §2.1). For \(P>1\) the preconditioner \(F_Z^{-1}\) is not a rescaling: it reduces iterations of the IQAN problem of Ch. 7 (median 58 → 22) at the cost of \(2P\) extra circuits per iteration (580 → 440 circuits; exact sim., hardware unverified).

9.4 Barren plateaus: a change of unit is not a mitigation
\(\mathrm{Var}[\partial_{\alpha}\mathcal L]_{\text{qga}}=(2\pi/1000)^2\,\mathrm{Var}[\partial_\theta\mathcal L]_{\text{rad}}\) for every loss and every \(n\) (exact). Status against for any claim of mitigation by qga/m-qga.

title: Chapter 10 — Geometric Phases and Stokes’ Theorem on the Sphere: Holonomy in qga, Bargmann Invariant and Single-Basis Readout
text:
10.1 Berry curvature as a charge-½ monopole in qga coordinates
Updated: November 15, 2026
With \(|\psi(\alpha,\varphi)\rangle=\cos\tfrac\theta2|0\rangle+e^{i\phi}\sin\tfrac\theta2|1\rangle\), \(\theta=2\pi\alpha/1000\), \(\phi=2\pi\varphi/1000\) (both in qga), the Berry connection and curvature are \[A=i\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle=-\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,d\phi=-\tfrac{1-qg_Z}{2}\,d\phi,\qquad F=dA=\tfrac12\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi .\] Stokes’ theorem: for every closed loop \(\mathcal C=\partial\Sigma\), \[\gamma=\oint_{\mathcal C}A=-\iint_\Sigma F=-\tfrac12\,\Omega(\Sigma),\] with \(\Omega\) the oriented solid angle. In the readout coordinate the 1-form is linear in \(qg_Z\): a latitude loop (one turn in \(\varphi\): \(1000\) qga) gives \[\gamma_{\text{lat}}=-\pi\,(1-qg_Z)\quad\text{[rad]}\qquad(\texttt{berry\_phase\_latitude}),\] so the geometric phase is read with a single basis (\(Z\)) and no ancilla (exact). Total curvature \(\iint_{S^2}F=2\pi\): charge \(\tfrac12\) (Ch. 1: the metric curvature of Fubini–Study \(=4\) is a different quantity; do not confuse them).

text:
10.2 Bargmann invariant and Pancharatnam phase
\[\gamma_{123}=\arg\big(\langle\psi_2|\psi_1\rangle\langle\psi_3|\psi_2\rangle\langle\psi_1|\psi_3\rangle\big)=-\tfrac12\,\Omega(\triangle_{123}),\qquad \Omega=2\arctan\frac{\mathbf r_1\cdot(\mathbf r_3\times\mathbf r_2)}{1+\mathbf r_1\!\cdot\mathbf r_2+\mathbf r_2\!\cdot\mathbf r_3+\mathbf r_3\!\cdot\mathbf r_1}\] (Van Oosterom–Strackee; \(\mathbf r_k\) = Bloch vectors \((qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\)). Gauge invariant to \(10^{-12}\) and convergent to the continuum limit as \(O(K^{-2})\) for a polygon of \(K\) vertices (exact). Convention fixed in code: \(\gamma=i\oint\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle\); with increasing \(\varphi\), \(\gamma<0\) and \(\Omega>0\).

10.3 Geometric Z gate versus virtual Z: a negative area finding
A relative phase \(\Omega\) between \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) (\(R_Z(\Omega)\)) is obtained (a) virtually: \(0\) pulses, \(0\) qga of area (Ch. 2); (b) physically: \(1\) pulse, area \(\Omega\cdot1000/2\pi\) qga; (c) geometrically by the loop pole \(\to(\theta,0)\to(\theta,\Delta\phi)\to\) pole: \(3\) pulses, area \((2\theta+d)\cdot1000/2\pi\) qga with \(d=\arccos(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos\Delta\phi)\). Instance (\(\theta=150\) qga, \(\Delta\phi=0.6\) rad): \(0\) / \(39.4\) / \(376.8\) qga. Status: area no gain (×9.6 worse than the physical one); holonomic robustness against amplitude noise stays unverified in this treatise (it is not claimed).

10.4 Shot budget for measuring γ
Latitude loop: \(\sigma_\gamma=\pi\,\sigma_{qg_Z}=\pi\sqrt{(1-qg_Z^2)/N}\) ⇒ \(N=\pi^2(1-qg_Z^2)/\sigma_\gamma^2\) (1 basis, 0 ancillas). General 3-state loop: tomography of \(\mathbf r_{1,2,3}\), \(\ge9\) measurement configurations. Note that the precision improves toward the poles (\(qg_Z\to\pm1\)), unlike the angular estimation of Ch. 9 (uniform in qga): \(\gamma\) is linear in \(qg_Z\), not in \(\alpha\).

title: Chapter 11 — Metrology in qga: Ramsey Operating Point, GHZ under Dephasing, tanh Thermometry and Clock Comparison
text:
11.1 Ramsey operating point in the readout coordinate
Updated: November 15, 2026
After the second \(\pi/2\) pulse the reading is \(qg_Z=C\cos\phi\), with \(C=e^{-T/T_2}\) the contrast and \(\phi=\omega T\). Fisher information per shot (Ch. 9): \[I_F(\phi)=\frac{C^2\sin^2\phi}{1-C^2\cos^2\phi}\ \le\ C^2,\qquad \text{equality at }\phi=\tfrac\pi2\iff qg_Z=0\ (250\text{ qga}).\] For \(C=1\) it is uniform (\(I_F\equiv1\), \(\sigma_{\text{qga}}=159.15/\sqrt N\)); for \(C<1\) the equator advantage is strict: operating at \(\phi=0.2\) rad loses 90 % (\(C=0.8\)) and 95 % (\(C=0.5\)) of the information. qang rule: fix the operating point by \(qg_Z=0\) read in m-qg, not by the nominal \(\phi\) (exact). Optimal time per unit time: \(\max_T T e^{-2T/T_2}\Rightarrow T^\star=T_2/2\). With finite contrast the equator (\(qg_Z=0\)) is the unique optimum; the operating point is set by the readout value, not by the nominal phase.

title: Chapter 11 — Metrology in qga: Ramsey Operating Point, GHZ under Dephasing, tanh Thermometry and Clock Comparison
section: 11.2 GHZ versus product under Markovian dephasing: no gain
text:
11.2 GHZ versus product under Markovian dephasing: no gain
Parity \(\langle X^{\otimes n}\rangle=e^{-nT/T_2}\cos n\phi\): \[\frac{I_F^{\text{GHZ}}(\omega)}{T}=n^2Te^{-2nT/T_2},\qquad \frac{I_F^{\text{prod}}(\omega)}{T}=nTe^{-2T/T_2},\qquad \max_T:\ \frac{nT_2}{2e}\ \text{in both cases}\ (T^\star_{\text{GHZ}}=\tfrac{T_2}{2n},\ T^\star_{\text{prod}}=\tfrac{T_2}{2}).\] Verified by optimal_T (descent in \(\log T\) with jax.grad) for \(n=2,5,10\) to \(10^{-9}\). At fixed \(T=T_2/2\) the \(n=5\) GHZ yields \(0.092\times\); it wins only if \(T<T_2\ln n/(2(n-1))\). Status no gain (Huelga et al. 1997 reproduced in qg coordinates); consistent with THEORY_CORE §2 (do not claim a Heisenberg advantage under Markovian noise).

11.3 One-qubit thermometry: qg_Z=tanh(x/2)
Gibbs state, \(x=\hbar\omega/k_BT\): \(qg_Z=\tanh(x/2)\) (§25). Fisher information per shot: \[I_F(x)=\frac{(\partial_xqg_Z)^2}{1-qg_Z^2}=\tfrac14\operatorname{sech}^2\tfrac x2,\qquad I_F(\ln T)=x^2I_F(x)\ \Rightarrow\ x^\star=2.399,\ qg_Z^\star=0.834\ (834\text{ m-qg}),\ I_F^\star=0.439 .\] The optimal sensor of relative temperature is therefore calibrated at a reading of \(834\) m-qg (exact); the delta method in \(p_0\) collapses near there (\(p_0=0.917\)), so use Bayes–Haar (Ch. 8).

13.1 Effective Hamiltonian and resonance in qga
Updated: November 15, 2026
In matter with electron density \(N_e\) the potential \(A=2\sqrt2G_FN_eE\) (\(=1.52\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{eV^2}\cdot(N_e/N_A\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}})\cdot E[\mathrm{GeV}]\)) tilts the effective mass axis: \[\cos2\theta_m=\frac{\cos2\theta-A/\Delta m^2}{\sqrt{(\cos2\theta-A/\Delta m^2)^2+\sin^22\theta}},\qquad \sin^22\theta_m=\frac{\sin^22\theta}{(\cos2\theta-A/\Delta m^2)^2+\sin^22\theta}.\] \(\cos2\theta_m\) is the \(qg_Z\) of the effective axis. The resonance \(A_{\text{res}}=\Delta m^2\cos2\theta\) is equivalent to \(\theta_m=\pi/4\): the effective axis crosses the equator (\(qg_Z=0\), \(250\) qga). For \(\theta_{12}\): \(2\theta_m\) goes from \(185.6\) qga (vacuum) to \(250.0\) qga (resonance); \(E_{\text{res}}=1.92\) MeV at \(N_e=100N_A\) cm\(^{-3}\) (exact). The MSW resonance is the equator crossing of the effective mass axis; \(\cos2\theta_m\) is literally the \(qg_Z\) of that axis.

13.5 JAX block (qang/qneutrino.py, matter part)
@jax.jit
def cos2theta_m(theta, dm2, A):              # qg_Z of the effective axis
    s, c = jnp.sin(2 * theta), jnp.cos(2 * theta); x = c - A / dm2
    return x / jnp.sqrt(x ** 2 + s ** 2)

@jax.jit
def adiabatic_survival_qz(theta, dm2, A_prod):   # qg_Z^{ee} = cos2θ_m(A_prod)·cos2θ
    return cos2theta_m(theta, dm2, A_prod) * jnp.cos(2 * theta)

def trotter_survival_qz(theta, dm2, E, A_profile, dL_km):   # lax.scan of arbitrary-axis rotations
    s, c = jnp.sin(2 * theta), jnp.cos(2 * theta)
    def step(psi, A):
        hz, hx = (-c + A / dm2), s; h = jnp.sqrt(hz ** 2 + hx ** 2)
        ang = 1.267 * dm2 * dL_km / E * h
        U = jnp.cos(ang) * jnp.eye(2) - 1j * jnp.sin(ang) * jnp.array([[hz, hx], [hx, -hz]]) / h
        return U @ psi, None
    psi, _ = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.array([1.0 + 0j, 0j]), A_profile)
    return 2.0 * jnp.abs(psi[0]) ** 2 - 1.0

14.1 Majorana phases: a virtual RZ that never reaches the readout
Updated: November 15, 2026
\(U=U_{\text{PMNS}}\,\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\alpha_{21}/2},e^{i\alpha_{31}/2})\). In the language of Ch. 2 and 12, the Majorana phases are \(R_Z\) rotations in the mass basis, which commute with the propagation \(R_Z(\phi_i)\) and cancel in \(|U_{\beta i}e^{-i\phi_i}U^*_{\alpha i}|^2\). Verified: \(P(\nu_\alpha\to\nu_\beta)\) invariant to \(10^{-14}\) for 9 pairs \((\alpha_{21},\alpha_{31};L/E)\) (exact). Operational consequence: no oscillation experiment, with or without qang, measures \(\alpha_{21},\alpha_{31}\); the m-qg readout is blind to them by construction.

\[|m_{\beta\beta}|=\Big|\sum_iU_{ei}^2m_i\Big|=\big|c_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_1+s_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_2e^{i\alpha_{21}}+s_{13}^2m_3e^{i(\alpha_{31}-2\delta)}\big| .\] Ranges (sweep \(\alpha_{21},\alpha_{31}\in[0,2\pi)\), \(73^2\) points): NO with \(m_{\text{light}}=0\): \([1.4,3.7]\) meV; NO with \(0.05\) eV: \([17.5,50.7]\) meV; IO with \(m_{\text{light}}=0\): \([18.8,48.5]\) meV. It is classical three-phasor arithmetic: status no gain (analogous to PQC, THEORY_CORE §2.6). qang contributes only the geometric reading (the three moduli \(|U_{ei}|^2m_i\) and their angles in qga), not a resource reduction.

text:
15.1 The Werner resource read in three correlators
Updated: November 15, 2026
\(\rho_V=V|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+|+(1-V)\tfrac{I}{4}\) has \(qg_{XX}=V\), \(qg_{YY}=-V\), \(qg_{ZZ}=V\) (Ch. 7: single-basis correlators each, 0 ancillas). Singlet fraction and mean teleportation fidelity (Horodecki): \[F_s=\tfrac14\big(1+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ}\big),\qquad \bar F=\frac{2F_s+1}{3},\qquad \bar F_{\text{Werner}}=\frac{1+V}{2}.\] Classical threshold \(\bar F=2/3\iff F_s=1/2\iff V=1/3\): the Bell pair is useful if and only if \(qg_{ZZ}>333\) m-qg under the Werner model (exact). For a general resource all 3 bases are needed; the single-basis reading is an upper bound (§15.4). The Werner resource is read as three single-basis correlators; the classical threshold is \(qg_{ZZ}=333\) m-qg under the Werner model, and an upper bound otherwise.

15.2 The teleportation channel in m-qg: m’=V m
Full teleportation (Bell measurement on input⊗A, Pauli correction on B) with resource \(\rho_V\) is the depolarizing channel \(\mathbf r\mapsto V\mathbf r\); in readout: \(m\text{-qg}'=V\cdot m\text{-qg}\) for any axis, verified to \(10^{-13}\) on random inputs. Example: \(+600\) m-qg \(\to+420\) (\(V=0.7\)) \(\to+200\) (\(V=1/3\)). The dissipative deficit of the teleported state (Ch. 5) is \(qg_\tau=\sqrt{1-V^2r^2}\). The average fidelity over the 2-design of 6 Pauli eigenstates reproduces \((1+V)/2\) to \(10^{-13}\) (exact).

title: Chapter 16 — Dual Rail, Loss as Heralded Erasure and Long-Distance Fidelity: Rate and Fidelity Decouple after the Sector Filter
text:
16.1 The dual-rail qubit lives in the Hamming-weight-1 sector
Updated: November 15, 2026
\(|0_L\rangle=|10\rangle\), \(|1_L\rangle=|01\rangle\) (modes \(a,b\)). Loss with transmission \(\eta=10^{-\alpha L/10}\) (\(\alpha=0.2\) dB/km) is amplitude damping independent per mode: weight leaves the sector \(\{|10\rangle,|01\rangle\}\) toward the vacuum \(|00\rangle\) and never mixes inside the sector. Therefore (exact): \[\text{without herald:}\quad qg_Z'=\eta\,qg_Z+(1-\eta)\ \ (\text{vacuum read as }0_L),\qquad \text{with sector filter:}\quad qg_Z'=qg_Z,\ \ \text{rate}=\eta .\] The bias without a filter is \((1-\eta)(1-qg_Z)\): at \(50\) km an input of \(-600\) m-qg reads \(+840\) m-qg; at \(200\) km, \(+1000\) m-qg (all information destroyed). With the filter the reading is exact at any distance, and so are \(qg_X,qg_Y\) (the postselected density matrix is \(\rho_L\)). Photon loss moves weight out of the Hamming-weight-1 sector without mixing inside it; sector postselection restores the full Bloch vector exactly at rate \(\eta\), while unheralded readout is biased by \((1-\eta)(1-qg_Z)\).

text:
16.2 Long-distance teleportation: loss costs rate, intra-sector noise costs fidelity
Werner pair \(V\) (Ch. 15) with one photon per arm: herald rate \(\eta(L/2)^2=\eta(L)\). After the filter, \(\bar F=(1+V)/2\) does not depend on \(L\); the shot budget is multiplied by \(1/\eta(L)\): \(\times10\) (50 km), \(\times100\) (100 km), \(\times10^4\) (200 km). The utility criterion remains \(qg_{ZZ}>333\) m-qg (Ch. 15) measured inside the sector. Design rule: optimize \(\eta\) and \(V\) separately; there is no trade-off between them after the filter (pure erasure model; dark counts and mode-dependent loss break the separation: mixed on hardware, §158).

17.1 The two maps
Updated: November 15, 2026
Let \(U\) be the interaction between the chronology-respecting qubit CR and the CTC qubit. \[\text{P-CTC (Lloyd):}\quad \rho\mapsto\frac{C\rho C^\dagger}{\mathrm{Tr}(C\rho C^\dagger)},\ \ C=\mathrm{Tr}_{\text{CTC}}U,\ \ p_{\text{post}}=\tfrac14\mathrm{Tr}(C\rho C^\dagger);\qquad \text{D-CTC (Deutsch):}\quad \rho_{\text{CTC}}=\mathrm{Tr}_{\text{CR}}\big[U(\rho\otimes\rho_{\text{CTC}})U^\dagger\big].\] P-CTC is the teleportation of Ch. 15 with the Bell measurement postselected: it costs one Bell pair (2 qubits) and \(\times1/p_{\text{post}}\) shots. D-CTC is a nonlinear fixed point (iteration from \(I/2\), maximum-entropy selection) with no single-circuit analogue. Both are simulated as maps and read in m-qg.

title: Chapter 18 — Black Holes as Scramblers: Hayden–Preskill, the P·F=1/4 Law of the Yoshida–Kitaev Decoder, OTOC and Why qgS Cannot See the Page Curve
text:
18.1 Probabilistic decoder and the identity P_EPR·F_EPR=1/d_A²
Updated: November 15, 2026
Message \(A\) (\(d_A=2\)) entangled with the reference \(R\); black hole \(B\) (\(n_B=3\)) maximally entangled with the early radiation \(B'\); dynamics \(U\) on \(AB\); late radiation \(D\) (\(n_D=2\)). The decoder applies \(U^*\) on \(A'B'\) (with \(A'R'\) in EPR) and projects \(DD'\) onto EPR: success with probability \(P_{\text{EPR}}\) and fidelity \(F_{\text{EPR}}=\langle\text{EPR}|\rho_{RR'}|\text{EPR}\rangle\). Identity (Yoshida–Kitaev): \[P_{\text{EPR}}\cdot F_{\text{EPR}}=\frac1{d_A^2}=\frac14\quad\text{for all }U,\] verified to \(10^{-12}\) for Haar \(U\) and \(U=I\). For Haar \(U\): \(P\approx d_A^{-2}+d_D^{-2}=0.3125\) (measured \(0.298\pm0.003\) with finite-size corrections), \(F\approx0.84\). The fidelity is read with three correlators of \((R,R')\) (Ch. 15): \(F=(1+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ})/4\), coinciding with the direct projection to \(10^{-12}\) (exact). Budget: \(\times1/P_{\text{EPR}}\approx3.4\) shots per heralded decoding. The probabilistic decoder obeys \(P\cdot F=1/d_A^2\) exactly; the fidelity is read from three \((R,R')\) correlators, no tomography.

title: Chapter 19 — Demarcation: Quantum Cryptography (QKD/QRNG) versus Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). Where There Is a Qubit to Read in m-qg and Where There Is None
text:
19.1 Demarcation criterion
Updated: November 15, 2026
qang measures angles and probabilities of physical qubits (Ch. 1). It applies where security rests on a projective readout: QKD (the QBER is a \(qg_Z\)) and QRNG (the min-entropy is a function of \(|qg_Z|\)). It does not apply to PQC (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, HQC): classical arithmetic on lattices/hashes/codes, with no qubit, with security parameters \(\delta\le2^{-138.8}\) whose “shot budget” would be \(N=(3/2\delta)^2=2^{278.8}\): uncountable (against, THEORY_CORE §2.6). A number that cannot be measured with shots is not an m-qg reading. qang applies where security rests on a projective readout of a physical qubit (QKD, QRNG) and not to PQC, whose security parameters are uncountable in shots.

20.1 The four states and the geometry of the bases
Updated: November 15, 2026
\(|Z_0\rangle,|Z_1\rangle\) at \(0\) and \(500\) qga (poles); \(|X_0\rangle,|X_1\rangle\) at \(250\) qga with \(\varphi=0,500\) qga (equator). \(|\langle Z_0|X_0\rangle|^2=\tfrac12\): mutually unbiased bases. text:
20.2 Intercept-resend and depolarizing channel in m-qg
Eve measures a fraction \(f\) of the pulses in \(Z\) or \(X\) at random and resends: \(e=f/4\) exactly (\(f=1\Rightarrow25\%\Leftrightarrow500\) m-qg). Depolarizing channel \(p\) without Eve: \(e=p/2\) (\(p=0.04\Rightarrow+960\) m-qg). Eve’s information (IR): \(I_E=f/2=2e\). Rates per sifted bit: \[r_{\text{IR}}=1-h(e)-2e,\qquad r_{\text{collective}}=1-2h(e)\ (\text{Ch. 19}),\qquad e^\star_{\text{col}}=0.110\Leftrightarrow780\text{ m-qg}\Leftrightarrow f^\star=0.44 .\] With \(f=0.5\): \(e=0.125\) (\(750\) m-qg), \(r_{\text{col}}=-0.087\) → abort, even though \(r_{\text{IR}}=+0.206\): the collective bound is the one that decides (exact).

text:
20.3 Sifted-bit budget
\(N=e(1-e)/\sigma_e^2\); \(\sigma_m=2000\,\sigma_e\) in m-qg. For \(\sigma_e=0.005\) (\(10\) m-qg): \(784\) bits at \(e=0.02\), \(2\,944\) at \(e=0.08\). Far from the pole (\(e\ge0.02\)) the delta method and Wilson coincide; near \(e\to0\) use Wilson/Bayes–Haar (Ch. 4, 21). 21.1 Point versus certificate
Updated: November 15, 2026
\(H_{\min}=-\log_2\frac{1+|qg_Z|}{2}\) (Ch. 19) evaluated at the point \(\hat{qg}_Z=2k_0/N-1\) overestimates: with \(k_0=N/2\) it gives \(1.000\) bit for any \(N\). The certified version takes the maximum of \(|qg_Z|\) over the \(99.9\%\) credible interval of the Bayes–Haar posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(1+k_0,1+N-k_0)\) (Ch. 8): \[H_{\min}^{\text{cert}}=-\log_2\frac{1+\max(|qg_Z^{\text{lo}}|,|qg_Z^{\text{hi}}|)}{2}:\quad N=10^3\to0.866,\ 10^4\to0.956,\ 10^5\to0.986,\ 10^6\to0.9955\ \text{bit}.\] Budget to certify \(H_{\min}\ge0.99\) (\(|qg_Z|\le7.0\) m-qg at \(99.9\%\)): \(N\approx1.97\cdot10^5\) shots (exact for the i.i.d. model). With a real bias of \(30\) m-qg (\(N=2\cdot10^5\)): point \(0.9528\), certified \(0.9431\), true \(0.9574\) — the certificate is a lower bound.

title: Chapter 22 — Quantum Batteries and Networks: Ergotropy as (r-qgZ)/2 and Repeater Chains with Visibility V^k
text:
22.1 Energy and ergotropy of a cell in qg
Updated: November 15, 2026
With \(H=\omega|1\rangle\langle1|\): \(E/\omega=(1-qg_Z)/2\) and, with \(r\) the local Bloch radius (Ch. 5), \[\frac{W}{\omega}=\frac{r-qg_Z}{2},\qquad \text{passive fraction}=\frac{1-r}{1-qg_Z}.\] Full charge \(qg_Z=-1\) (\(-1000\) m-qg): \(W=\omega\). Finding: the \(Z\) reading alone does not determine the extractable charge: \(|+\rangle\) (\(0\) m-qg, \(r=1\)) has \(W=\omega/2\); \(I/2\) (\(0\) m-qg, \(r=0\)) has \(W=0\). Ergotropy requires \(r\) (3 bases or unbiased squares, THEORY_CORE §1), just like \(qg_\tau\) (exact). Collective versus parallel charging power: unverified here (no advantage is claimed). Ergotropy is \((r-qg_Z)/2\) in units of \(\omega\); the \(Z\) readout alone cannot distinguish a coherent half-charged cell from a passive one.

A chain of \(k\) Werner links \(V\) with ideal Bell measurements: the composite channel is depolarizing with \(V_{\text{end}}=V^k\) (verified numerically \(0.9\times0.8=0.720\): \(qg_{ZZ}=720\) m-qg). Utility (Ch. 15): \(V^k>1/3\) ⇒ \(k_{\max}=\lfloor\ln(1/3)/\ln V\rfloor\): \(V=0.99\to109\) links (\(334\) m-qg), \(0.95\to21\), \(0.9\to10\) (\(349\) m-qg; the 11th falls to \(314\)), \(0.8\to4\). Network planning: measure \(qg_{ZZ}\) per link (1 basis), multiply, compare with \(333\) m-qg (exact for Werner; non-Werner states: upper bound, Ch. 15 §4). Loss per link: rate \(\times\eta^k\) (Ch. 16), not fidelity.

title: Chapter 23 — Weight-Preserving Quantum Neural Networks: Unary Loader, RBS Gates in qga, Symmetry Filter under T1 and QSP as a Chebyshev Polynomial in qg
text:
23.1 Weight-1 sector: unary loader and RBS gates
Updated: November 15, 2026
A unit vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is loaded as \(|x\rangle=\sum_kx_k|e_k\rangle\) in the Hamming-weight-1 sector with \(n-1\) RBS (Givens) gates — exact to \(10^{-13}\), including the sign of the last component. The network is a sequence of \(\mathrm{RBS}(\theta_k)\) with \(\theta_k\) in qga on adjacent pairs; it conserves the weight exactly (mass outside the sector \(=0\) to machine precision) and realizes a rotation \(O\in SO(n)\) of the sector (universal: 9 RBS on \((0,1),(2,3),(1,2)\times3\) fit any \(O\in SO(4)\) to \(10^{-30}\)). Reading: \(y=\sum_{k\in A}p(e_k)-\sum_{k\notin A}p(e_k)=x^\top O^\top DO\,x\), a quadratic form with spectrum \((\pm1)\) (exact). The same sector as in Ch. 12 (3 flavors), 14 (sterile) and 16 (dual rail). The unary loader and RBS layers keep the state in the weight-1 sector exactly; the classifier output is a quadratic form read from \(n\) probabilities of one \(Z\) histogram.

Uniform \(T_1\) relaxation \(\gamma\) on the histogram: without a filter \(y\to(1-\gamma)y\); with a sector filter \(y\) is exact with acceptance rate \((1-\gamma)\). Shots to confirm the sign at \(3\sigma\) (Ch. 1, \(N_{\text{sign}}\)): \(\gamma=0.3\): without filter \(63\), with filter \(44\) ⇒ \(\times1.43=1/(1-\gamma)\) (exact).
